blindSummary: The most concentrated wave of mob violence against transgender women recorded in the country: ten attacks on 45 victim-survivors in a major city between 30 March and 15 July 2026, documented by a local LGBTI monitoring group — groups of 10–20 men punched, kicked, threw stones, glass bottles and firecrackers at trans women and stripped some of them naked, filming the assaults for social media under a branded anti-LGBT account. No alleged perpetrator has been publicly identified, arrested or prosecuted; a trans-rights activist who accompanied women filing police reports said officers 'accepted the case but worked on it half-heartedly,' and some survivors were too afraid to report. Separately, on 22 June 2025 police detained 75 people at a villa raid in a mountain district at a gathering labelled a 'gay party' that violated no law; a global human-rights organisation demanded their release. Activists attribute the violence's legitimisation to a 2025 presidential regulation, which from October 2025 lists 'LGBTQ culture' as a national-resilience threat alongside terrorism and drug abuse: 'people feel able to commit violence arbitrarily because they believe the state has legitimised that violence.' The pattern-plus-impunity combination is specific to this state/province; national same-sex criminalisation does not by itself explain the street-vigilante wave with total state inaction and explicit anti-trans branding over four months.

A national news magazine (June 2025): police detained 75 people at a villa in a mountain district of this state/province after an alleged LGBT gathering — police framed it as a moral offence though no law was violated.

A global human-rights organisation (June 2025): demands release of the 75 people detained in the mountain-villa raid, calling it a discriminatory raid on a 'gay party' and noting the gathering violated no law and posed no threat — documenting police mass-detention practice in this state/province.
